_comment: Per-state income-tax constants. SOURCE OF TRUTH for both the TypeScript engine (stateTaxRules.ts) and scripts/verify_plan.py — JSON so there is one file and two readers, no hand-duplication. Every constant must be verifiable against the primary source in `sources`. Review annually: see docs/5-state-tax-model.md.

CA.note: California indexes brackets, the standard deduction, and the exemption credit to the California CPI each year (R&TC §17041(h)), but the adjustment factor for a given tax year depends on CPI data through June of THAT year (§17041(h)(1)) — so unlike GA/VA's forward-enacted schedules, CA's current-year figures cannot be finalized in advance. FTB's own 2026 Form 540-ES instructions confirm this: they direct taxpayers estimating 2026 tax to use the 2025 rate table and the 2025 exemption credit amount. This entry therefore uses TY2025's closed-out, fully confirmed figures (dated accordingly) rather than a projection. Bracket dollar thresholds were cross-derived from EDD's official 2026 payroll withholding schedule, whose Method B tables publish rates at exactly 1.1x the real marginal rate (a known CA withholding markup); dividing back out recovers the statutory brackets, and the extra breakpoint the withholding table inserts for married filers independently confirms the Behavioral Health Services Tax's $1,000,000 threshold is NOT doubled for joint returns (it lands at $1,000,000 combined, not $2,000,000). The exemption credit ($168 / $168 senior addition) is likewise EDD's Table 4 allowance-credit figure rather than a direct FTB Form 540 citation, since ftb.ca.gov blocks automated fetches; R&TC §17054(c) confirms the senior addition shares the same $52 (1987) base and the same annual indexing clause as the base personal credit in §17054(a), so the two must be equal in any given year. Not modeled: the dependent exemption credit and the blind exemption (retirees rarely have dependents — same reasoning as Georgia's unmodeled dependent exemption, docs/5-state-tax-model.md §6). Capital gains are taxed as ordinary income — California has no preferential rate.
CA.caveat: California's bracket, standard-deduction, and exemption-credit figures are indexed to California CPI but cannot be finalized until partway through the year they cover, so this plan uses the last officially confirmed tax year (2025) — the true current-year figures, once published, will differ modestly (CA's own inflation adjustment is typically 2-4%/year). California also levies a 1% Behavioral Health Services Tax (formerly the Mental Health Services Tax) on taxable income above $1,000,000 — a threshold that does NOT double for joint filers, a real marriage penalty at that income level.

GA.note: HB 463's further rate cuts (-0.125%/yr toward a 3.99% floor) and standard-deduction increases (+$375/+$750/yr) are CONTINGENT on revenue triggers, so both are frozen at their TY2026 values — see docs/5-state-tax-model.md §2 Rule 1. The TY2027 exclusion step-up to $70,000 is unconditional in the same bill, so it IS modeled. No age-65 addition to the standard deduction exists under the flat-tax structure. Constants come from the enacted bill text and IT-511, NOT the DoR web pages, which are stale and contradict each other on the earned-income sublimit.
GA.caveat: Georgia tax is likely overstated: HB 463's scheduled rate cuts and standard-deduction increases depend on state revenue triggers, so both stay frozen at TY2026 values (4.99%; $15,000 single / $30,000 married). Note that tax-smart withdrawals sized to the federal deduction floor can still owe Georgia tax before age 62, when the retirement exclusion has not yet begun. For couples, the per-person exclusion is applied to pooled household income, which over-excludes when only one spouse has retirement income.

NH.note: The Interest & Dividends Tax was repealed effective 1 Jan 2025 (HB 2, 2023 session), so NH taxes no individual income for TY2026 onward.

NY.note: Brackets are TY2026 (Chapter 59, Laws of 2025 cut the bottom five rates 0.1pp starting TY2026; a further 0.1pp cut is enacted for TY2027 — Rule 1 unconditional, model as it arrives). The published 9-rate schedule (3.90%/4.40%/5.15%/5.40%/5.90%/6.85%/9.65%/10.30%/10.90%) only applies below $107,650 of NY AGI (NOT doubled for MFJ); above it, NY recaptures the benefit of its own lower brackets via a supplemental tax phased in over $50,000-wide bands, escalating toward a flat 10.90% above $25,000,000. Rather than reimplement that worksheet mechanism, the recapture is resolved into extra rows of the ordinary bracket table directly from NY DTF's own official NYS-50-T-NYS (1/26) withholding publication, whose annualized 'Method II Exact Calculation' tables already flatten it into a cumulative bracket schedule (confirmed by checking that each row's base dollar amount equals the running total of prior rows, the same convention Virginia's schedule uses) — this is why several middle brackets look non-monotonic (e.g. single: 5.90% -> 7.03% -> 7.53% -> 6.40% -> 11.44% -> 7.35%). The three brackets above $1,077,550 single / $2,155,350 married (9.65%/10.30%/10.90%) are DERIVED, not directly quoted: NY's own withholding 'Method III' top-rate method uses different, deliberately over-withheld rates (10.45%/11.10%/11.70%, a flat +0.80pp payroll safety margin analogous in purpose to California's 1.1x EDD markup, confirmed by comparing Method III's discontinuous jump against Method II's own formula at the boundary) that do not reflect true liability, so the true published top rates were continued instead, anchored to be continuous with Method II's last row. That income level is far beyond this tool's audience regardless. Government pensions (NYS, local government, federal, and military, Tax Law §612(c)(3)) are fully exempt with no cap and no age test. Private pension, annuity, and IRA/tax-deferred income instead gets a $20,000-per-qualifying-person exclusion (Tax Law §612(c)(3-a), unchanged since 1981), age 59½+ — modeled as 60 because the engine's simulated age has no fractional/mid-year precision (docs/5-state-tax-model.md §4.5); this rounds the exclusion's start up by up to a year, understating the exclusion and overstating tax, the same conservative direction as this project's other simplifications. The exclusion is per person and NOT poolable across spouses ('neither of you can claim any unused part of your spouse's exclusion', IT-201-I), and covers IRA lump-sum and periodic distributions in addition to employer pensions and annuities — so it is checked against private pension income AND tax-deferred withdrawals combined, not pensions alone. Not modeled: the $1,000 dependent exemption (retirees rarely have dependents, same reasoning as Georgia's and California's unmodeled dependent exemptions), NYC and Yonkers local income tax, and the Metropolitan Commuter Transportation Mobility Tax (self-employment only, not applicable to retirement income). Standard deduction is fixed by statute (Tax Law §614), not inflation-indexed, and has been $8,000/$16,050 since at least 2018 — held flat like Georgia's and Virginia's.
NY.caveat: New York's brackets look unusual in the middle of the schedule (dipping and spiking) because above $107,650 of combined income (not doubled for married filers), New York claws back the benefit of its own lower tax brackets in $50,000-wide steps — a real effect for many NY retirees, not just very high earners. Government pensions (NYS, local, federal, military) are fully tax-exempt; private pensions, annuities, and IRA withdrawals get a combined $20,000-per-person exclusion instead, available once you're near 60. New York City and Yonkers residents owe additional local income tax that this plan does not compute.

TN.note: The Hall income tax on interest and dividends was fully repealed for tax years beginning 1 Jan 2021.

VA.note: The entire Virginia schedule is unconditional, so Rule 1 models all of it including the 2030 standard-deduction reversion to $3,000/$6,000 (docs/5-state-tax-model.md §2). Virginia has repeatedly extended the elevated deduction rather than let it lapse, so the cliff may never happen — modeling it is the current-law reading, not a forecast. The age deduction is a HOUSEHOLD-level means test against a pooled cap, which maps cleanly onto this tool's pooled MFJ accounts (unlike Georgia's per-person exclusion). Its dollar-for-dollar phase-out doubles the marginal rate to ~11.5% inside the band, which is why the withdrawal gross-up takes the whole state formula as a function rather than one rate (§3). Not modeled: the separate $12,000 deduction for taxpayers born on or before 1 Jan 1939 (they are 87+ in 2026 and it needs a birth year, not an age), the blindness exemption, the military benefits subtraction, and dependent exemptions. Brackets and the $930/$800 exemptions are NOT inflation-indexed in statute, so they are held flat.
VA.caveat: Virginia's standard deduction is modeled as reverting to $3,000 single / $6,000 married in 2030, which is what current law says but which the legislature has repeatedly postponed — so Virginia tax is likely overstated from 2030 on. The $12,000-per-person age deduction starts at 65, not at retirement, and phases out $1 per $1 of income above $50,000 single / $75,000 married; inside that band each extra dollar withdrawn is taxed at roughly 11.5% rather than 5.75%. Virginia has no general pension or 401(k)/IRA exclusion — the age deduction is the only retiree benefit, and there is none at all before 65.

WA.caveat: Washington has no income tax, but levies a 7% excise tax on long-term capital gains above an inflation-indexed standard deduction ($278,000 for 2025), with an additional higher tier. It is NOT modeled here: retirement accounts are exempt, so it reaches only taxable-brokerage gains, and this tool applies a flat cost-basis percentage per withdrawal rather than tracking realized gains.
